headline: Bank of England raises rate to 4% and warns inflation could reach about 5% by mid-2027

terms.meaning: The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences what banks charge on loans and pay on savings.
The nine-member Bank of England group that votes on interest rates.
One hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 basis points is 0.25%.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises rate to 4% and warns inflation could reach about 5% by mid-2027
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its base rate by 25 basis points, from 3.75% to 4%, on 5 November. It was the first increase since August 2023. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1, with one member wanting a larger rise of 50 basis points to 4.25%.
The Bank now expects UK inflation to climb to about 5% by the middle of 2027. The latest official figure from the Office for National Statistics put CPI inflation at 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% in August, with transport costs a main driver. The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
Governor Andrew Bailey said he could see the argument for a further rise unless energy price risks ease. Markets were pricing roughly a one-in-four chance of another increase at the next decision on 17 December. HMRC has said its interest rates on late and overpaid tax will be revised to match, from 16 November for quarterly instalment payments and 24 November for other instalments.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs and faster price rises affect mortgages, savings and the cost of living for most households.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts interest rates to 4% and says inflation could approach 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England increased Bank Rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% on 5 November, its first rise since August 2023. Eight members of the Monetary Policy Committee backed the move, while one argued for a bigger half-point increase.
Policymakers now think inflation will rise to about 5% by the middle of next year. In September, official figures showed consumer price inflation at 3.5%, up from 3.1% a month earlier, mainly because transport prices rose. New figures are due on 18 November.
Governor Andrew Bailey told reporters he could see the case for more increases if energy price risks do not fade. Financial markets saw about a 25% chance of a further rise when the Bank next meets on 17 December. HMRC will also raise the interest it charges on late tax payments, starting on 16 November for some instalments.
levels.why: Interest rate decisions shape what people pay on loans and mortgages and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Interest rates go up to 4% as the Bank of England warns prices could rise faster
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. This is the first rise since August 2023. Eight of the nine people on the committee that decides rates voted for it, and one wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank said it expects inflation, the rate at which prices go up, to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. In September it was 3.5%, up from 3.1% in August, partly because transport costs rose.
Governor Andrew Bailey said he could see the argument for another rise unless risks to energy prices ease. Markets think there is about a one in four chance of that happening at the next decision on 17 December. The tax authority, HMRC, will also change the interest it charges on late tax payments to match.
levels.why: Many families and businesses will feel the change through the cost of borrowing and the price of everyday goods.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% because it fears prices will rise faster
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate to 4%, up from 3.75%. It is the first increase in more than two years. Eight of the nine members of the committee that sets the rate voted yes, and one wanted an even bigger rise.
The reason is inflation, which means prices going up over time. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year before. The Bank thinks that figure could reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, which tends to slow spending and so can help to cool price rises.
Governor Andrew Bailey said another rise is possible if energy price worries do not ease. The next decision is on 17 December. The tax office, HMRC, will also raise what it charges for late tax payments.
levels.why: If you borrow money, such as a mortgage, it may cost more, while savers may earn a little more.

levels.headline: Interest rates rise to 4%: the Bank of England says prices could go up faster
levels.body:
The Bank of England has made borrowing a little more expensive. Its key interest rate, which affects what banks charge on loans and pay on savings, has gone up from 3.75% to 4%. Eight of the nine people who vote on it agreed. One wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank did this because it is worried about inflation. Inflation is how quickly prices rise. In September it was 3.5%, which is higher than the month before. The Bank thinks it could reach about 5% by the middle of next year, which is well above its usual aim.
The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said more rises could follow if energy costs stay a worry. The next decision is on 17 December, and the tax office will change its rates on late payments too.
levels.why: Prices and loan costs touch almost everyone, from shoppers to people with a mortgage.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raises interest rates and says prices may climb faster
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. The Bank is where the country's rate for borrowing money is set. Eight of the nine members of its rate-setting group voted for the rise. One wanted it to be bigger.
The main worry is rising prices, which is called inflation. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. The Bank thinks that could reach about 5% by the middle of next year. Raising rates makes loans cost more, so people tend to spend less, and that helps slow price rises.
The Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey, said another rise could come if energy costs stay a concern. The next decision is on 17 December. The tax office will also charge more on late tax payments.
levels.why: Anyone with a loan or a mortgage could pay more, while people who save may earn more.

levels.headline: The Bank of England puts up interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates. They went up from 3.75% to 4%. This is the first rise since 2023.
The Bank did it because prices are rising faster. Inflation means the cost of things like food, fuel and travel goes up over time. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. The Bank thinks it could reach about 5% next year.
When interest rates go up, borrowing money costs more. People spend a bit less, and that can slow price rises down. Savers may get paid more by their banks.
The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said another rise could come if energy prices stay a worry. The Bank will decide again on 17 December. Most of its voters, eight out of nine, agreed with this rise.
levels.why: It could change how much families pay each month on loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: Interest rates go up and prices may rise faster
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow, or the extra money a bank pays you when you save.
Why do it now? Prices are going up quickly. This is called inflation. A year ago, a snack might have cost a pound. Now it might cost a little more. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year before, and the Bank thinks they could go up by about 5% next year.
When borrowing costs more, people tend to spend less, and prices can stop rising so fast. Eight out of nine experts on the Bank's committee voted for the change. The next decision is on 17 December. The boss, Andrew Bailey, said more rises are possible.
levels.why: It affects the cost of mortgages and loans that families pay, and what savers earn.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the bank for the whole country. This week it made borrowing money cost more. The cost of borrowing is called the interest rate. It went up from 3.75 to 4 out of every 100 pounds each year.
Why? Prices have been going up. When prices go up over time, we call it inflation. Last year, a pound bought more than it does now. The Bank thinks prices could keep going up and may rise by about 5% by the middle of next year.
Making borrowing dearer can slow things down. People spend less, so prices stop climbing so fast. Eight of nine people on the Bank's team voted yes. They will decide again on 17 December. Their boss, Andrew Bailey, said they might raise rates again.
levels.why: Families who borrow money may pay a bit more, and people who save may earn a bit more.

levels.headline: The people who look after our money made a change
levels.body:
Think of the Bank of England as the grown-up who looks after the country's money. This week it made a change. It made borrowing money a little more expensive.
Imagine you borrow a toy from a friend and promise to give back the toy plus a small extra gift. That extra gift is like interest. The Bank made the extra gift a bit bigger.
Why? Because things in shops have been getting more expensive, like when sweets cost more pocket money than before. The Bank is worried they might cost even more soon. When borrowing costs more, people spend a little less, and prices can stop climbing so fast.
The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said they may do it again if they need to. They will think about it again on 17 December.
levels.why: Grown-ups pay more when they borrow, which can change how much money families have for treats.

headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.38% at 7,520.93 as hot inflation data fuels rate-hike fears

terms.meaning: An index tracking 500 large US companies, used to judge how the stock market is doing.
A measure of how fast prices for everyday goods and services are rising.
The central bank of the United States, which sets US interest rates.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.38% at 7,520.93 as hot inflation data fuels rate-hike fears
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down 0.38% at 7,520.93 on Tuesday 10 November, its first negative session in three. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3% to 52,231.89, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.74% to 25,065.87. Nvidia was the biggest drag on the market. This was the last completed session before this edition.
Stocks fell after October's US consumer price index came in hotter than forecast. Prices rose 0.4% on the month against 0.3% expected, and core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3% against 0.2%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics published no annual rate, because October 2025 data were not collected during the government shutdown.
Traders now fully price a quarter-point Federal Reserve rate rise at its 8 to 9 December meeting. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she sees a need for two more quarter-point increases. The Fed's range is currently 3.75% to 4%. The fall followed Monday's 2.35% jump to 7,549.94.
levels.why: US share prices and interest rate expectations ripple through pensions, savings and borrowing costs worldwide.

levels.headline: Wall Street falls after hotter US inflation figures raise the prospect of more Fed rate rises
levels.body:
US shares fell on Tuesday 10 November. The S&P 500 closed down 0.38% at 7,520.93, the Dow lost 0.3% to finish at 52,231.89 and the Nasdaq fell 0.74% to 25,065.87. Nvidia was the biggest drag. It was the most recent completed trading session.
The fall came after US consumer prices for October rose 0.4% on the month, ahead of the 0.3% economists expected, with core prices up 0.3% rather than 0.2%. No annual figure was published because data for October 2025 were never collected during a government shutdown.
Investors now fully expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates by a quarter of a point at its 8 to 9 December meeting. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she sees a need for two more quarter-point rises. The Fed's policy range is currently 3.75% to 4%. On Monday the S&P 500 had jumped 2.35%.
levels.why: Expectations for US interest rates influence mortgage costs, savings returns and markets around the world.

levels.headline: US stocks end lower on Tuesday after prices rise faster than expected
levels.body:
US stock markets closed lower on Tuesday 10 November, the latest completed trading day. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big companies, fell 0.38% to 7,520.93. The Dow Jones lost 0.3% to close at 52,231.89, and the Nasdaq dropped 0.74% to 25,065.87. Chipmaker Nvidia pulled the market down most.
The fall came after new figures showed US prices rose 0.4% in October, more than the 0.3% experts expected. Prices not counting food and energy rose 0.3%. That worried investors that the US central bank, the Federal Reserve, will keep raising interest rates.
Traders now expect a quarter-point rise on 8 to 9 December. One Fed official, Lorie Logan, said she thinks two more rises may be needed. Shares had jumped 2.35% the day before.
levels.why: What happens to US shares and rates can affect savings, pensions and prices in the UK too.

levels.headline: US shares fall as prices rise faster than expected
levels.body:
US shares ended lower on Tuesday 10 November. The S&P 500 index, which follows 500 large companies, closed down 0.38% at 7,520.93. The Dow Jones fell 0.3% to 52,231.89 and the Nasdaq slipped 0.74% to 25,065.87. A big chipmaker, Nvidia, was the biggest drag.
The reason was new inflation news. Inflation means prices rising over time. Prices in the US went up 0.4% in October, which is more than the 0.3% experts had guessed. That makes some investors think the US central bank, called the Federal Reserve, may put up interest rates again.
Traders now expect a rise of a quarter of a point in early December. A Fed official, Lorie Logan, said she thinks two more rises could be needed. Higher rates make borrowing dearer and can pull share prices down.
levels.why: US interest rates affect the whole world's markets, including the value of pensions and savings.

levels.headline: US shares slip as new figures show prices rising faster than expected
levels.body:
US shares went down on Tuesday 10 November. The S&P 500, a measure of 500 big companies, fell 0.38% to 7,520.93. The Dow Jones lost 0.3% and the Nasdaq lost 0.74%. The chipmaker Nvidia was the biggest drag.
The cause was a report on prices. Prices in the US rose 0.4% in October, faster than the 0.3% experts expected. Prices not counting food and energy rose 0.3%. This matters because it makes it more likely that the US central bank, the Federal Reserve, will raise interest rates again.
Traders now expect a rise of a quarter of a point on 8 to 9 December. A Fed official, Lorie Logan, said she thinks two more rises could be needed. Higher interest rates can make shares less attractive, so some investors sold.
levels.why: US markets influence pensions, savings and borrowing costs well beyond America.

levels.headline: US shares fall and investors worry about higher interest rates
levels.body:
US share prices fell on Tuesday 10 November. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies, closed down 0.38% at 7,520.93. Two other measures, the Dow Jones and the Nasdaq, fell as well. A chip company called Nvidia pulled the market down most.
Investors were reacting to a report that showed prices in the US rising by 0.4% in October. That is more than experts had expected. When prices rise quickly, the country's central bank, the Federal Reserve, can raise interest rates to cool things down. Traders now think it will do that in December.
Higher interest rates make it dearer to borrow money. That can mean companies make less profit, so some people sell their shares. The day before, shares had risen a lot, so this was a step back.
levels.why: Interest rates in America can affect savings and prices in other countries too.

levels.headline: US share prices drop after a report shows prices rising faster
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States went down on Tuesday 10 November. A share is a small piece of a company. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big companies, fell 0.38% to 7,520.93. The Dow Jones fell 0.3% and the Nasdaq fell 0.74%. Both are other ways of measuring the market. The chip company Nvidia was a big reason for the fall.
A new report showed that prices in the US rose 0.4% in October. Experts had expected 0.3%, so this was worse than hoped. When prices climb fast, the US bank that sets interest rates, the Federal Reserve, may raise rates to slow things down.
Investors now think a rise of a quarter of a point is coming in December. Higher rates can make companies less valuable, so people sell shares.
levels.why: Stock markets can affect pensions and savings, and US decisions often reach the UK.

levels.headline: American shares fall a little after prices rise faster
levels.body:
On Tuesday 10 November, shares in American companies went down a little. Shares are tiny parts of a company that people can buy. One way to measure them is the S&P 500, which follows 500 big firms. It fell by 0.38%, to 7,520.93. Two other measures, the Dow Jones and the Nasdaq, fell too.
The day before, shares had gone up a lot. So Tuesday was a small step back.
The cause was news about prices. In the US, prices rose 0.4% in October. That is faster than experts thought. When prices rise fast, the bank in charge of interest rates, called the Fed, may make borrowing cost more. Investors expect this might happen in December.
Costlier borrowing can make companies earn less, so some people sold their shares.
levels.why: What happens to big American firms can touch savings and pensions far away.

levels.headline: Share prices dip in America after bad news about prices
levels.body:
On Tuesday, share prices in the United States went down a little. A share is a tiny piece of a company. If lots of people want to sell their pieces, the price goes down.
There is a list called the S&P 500 that follows 500 large companies. It fell by 0.38%. That is a small fall, less than half of one penny in each pound. Two other lists, the Dow Jones and the Nasdaq, fell too.
Why? New figures showed that prices in shops and for bills went up faster than experts thought. This is called inflation. The bank in charge of money in America, the Fed, may now raise interest rates. That makes borrowing cost more, and companies may earn less. So some people sold shares.
levels.why: Prices and interest rates matter because they change how far money stretches.

levels.headline: Share prices fall a little in America
levels.body:
Imagine a big market where people buy and sell tiny pieces of companies. These pieces are called shares. On Tuesday, more people wanted to sell than buy, so prices went down a little.
A list called the S&P 500 follows 500 big companies. It went down by 0.38%. That is like a pound coin losing less than half a penny. The day before, it had gone up a lot, so this was a small step back.
Why did it happen? The cost of things in America went up faster than people hoped. When that happens, the bank that looks after American money, the Fed, may make borrowing cost more. People worry that firms will earn less, so some sold shares.
levels.why: Money news from a big country can reach other places and change what people earn and pay.

headline: Trump says Iran war is 'effectively over' and will end 'fairly soon' as Tehran denies planned talks

terms.meaning: Using warships to stop ships entering or leaving a place.
A narrow sea route in the Gulf through which a large share of the world's oil ships.
US elections held halfway through a president's term, mainly for Congress.

levels.headline: Trump says Iran war is 'effectively over' and will end 'fairly soon' as Tehran denies planned talks
levels.body:
President Donald Trump said on 9 and 10 November that the war with Iran could end "fairly soon", describing it as "militarily, effectively over" and new strikes as "quite unlikely", while saying the US was ready to act if needed. The US naval blockade and the "Operation Iron Gate" land task force remain in place.
Iran's Foreign Minister denied that any meeting was being planned. Tasnim reported that Tehran would not hold talks until Washington took concrete steps within the framework of Iran's seven conditions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reported no progress, and Qatar said it could not say how close an agreement was.
Analyst Fereidun Fesharaki said the two sides were too far apart to bridge, arguing Iran would not restore pre-war oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Trump's softer tone followed midterm elections in which Republicans lost both chambers of Congress. Earlier ceasefire and deal claims this year have fallen through.
levels.why: The war has disrupted oil supplies and raised prices worldwide, so any end or escalation affects household costs.

levels.headline: Trump says the Iran war is 'effectively over', but Tehran denies talks are planned
levels.body:
Donald Trump said on 9 and 10 November that the Iran war could end "fairly soon". He called it "militarily, effectively over" and said fresh strikes were "quite unlikely", while insisting the US could act again if needed. The naval blockade and the "Operation Iron Gate" task force are still in place.
Iran's foreign minister denied any meeting was planned, and Tasnim said Tehran would only talk after Washington took concrete steps under Iran's seven conditions. Marco Rubio reported no progress, and Qatar would not say how near a deal was.
Analyst Fereidun Fesharaki argued the gap between the sides cannot be bridged, since Iran is unlikely to restore pre-war oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Mr Trump's tone has softened since Republicans lost both houses of Congress in the midterms. Previous claims of ceasefires and deals this year have collapsed.
levels.why: A lasting settlement or a new round of fighting would shape fuel prices and global security.

levels.headline: Trump says the Iran war is almost over, but Iran says no talks are planned
levels.body:
President Donald Trump said this week that the war with Iran could end "fairly soon". He said it was "militarily, effectively over" and that more strikes were "quite unlikely", though the US would act if it had to. American ships are still blockading Iran, and a land task force called "Operation Iron Gate" remains in place.
Iran's foreign minister said no meeting was planned. Iranian media said Tehran will not talk until the US takes steps that meet Iran's seven conditions. The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, said there had been no progress, and Qatar said it could not tell how close a deal was.
One analyst said the two sides are too far apart. Mr Trump's tone changed after his party lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. Earlier hopes of a deal this year have failed.
levels.why: The war has pushed up the cost of oil and fuel, so peace or more fighting matters for prices everywhere.

levels.headline: Trump says the Iran war is nearly over, but Iran does not agree that talks are happening
levels.body:
US President Donald Trump has said the war with Iran could end "fairly soon". He described it as "effectively over" in military terms and said more attacks were unlikely, but he added that the US could strike again if needed. American warships are still blocking Iranian ports, and a land force remains in place.
Iran says no meeting is planned. Its news agency said the country will only talk if the US meets Iran's seven conditions. America's top diplomat, Marco Rubio, said talks have made no progress. Qatar, which has been helping, said it could not say how close a deal is.
One expert said the two sides are too far apart. Mr Trump's mood has softened since his party lost both parts of Congress in elections last week. Earlier promises of a deal this year came to nothing.
levels.why: The conflict has made oil and fuel more expensive, so the outcome affects people far from the Middle East.

levels.headline: Trump says the war with Iran is nearly over, but Iran says there are no talks
levels.body:
The American president, Donald Trump, says the war with Iran may end "fairly soon". He says the fighting is "effectively over" and that new attacks are unlikely. But he says America could strike again if it needs to. American ships are still stopping boats from reaching Iran, which is called a blockade.
Iran says no meeting is planned. It says it will only talk if America does certain things first, which Iran calls its seven conditions. America's top diplomat, Marco Rubio, said talks have not moved forward. Qatar, a country helping to pass messages, would not say how close a deal is.
An expert said the two sides are very far apart. Earlier this month, Mr Trump's party lost control of Congress in elections. Earlier hopes of a deal this year did not come true.
levels.why: The war has made oil dearer, so what happens next could change petrol and energy prices.

levels.headline: Trump says the war with Iran is nearly over, but Iran says no talks are planned
levels.body:
The American president, Donald Trump, says the war with Iran could end "fairly soon". He says it is "effectively over" and that more attacks are unlikely, but America could strike again if it needed to. American ships are still blocking Iranian ports.
Iran says no meeting is planned. It says it will talk only if America meets seven conditions. The American Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, said talks had made no progress. Qatar, which is helping, said it could not say how close a deal was.
One expert said the two sides are too far apart. Mr Trump has sounded softer since his party lost control of Congress in elections. Earlier promises of a deal this year have failed.
levels.why: The war has pushed up fuel costs, so peace or more fighting matters to families everywhere.

levels.headline: Trump says the Iran war is almost finished, but Iran says it is not talking
levels.body:
The war between America and Iran has gone on for months. This week the American president, Donald Trump, said it could end "fairly soon". He said new attacks were unlikely, but that America could still attack if it needed to.
Iran does not agree that talks are coming. Its foreign minister said no meeting was planned. Iran says it will only talk if America does certain things first. America's top diplomat, Marco Rubio, said talks had not moved forward.
A blockade is when ships are used to stop other ships coming in or out. American ships are still doing this near Iran. The war has also hurt oil supplies, because oil travels by ship through a narrow sea called the Strait of Hormuz.
One expert said the two sides are still too far apart. Earlier hopes of a deal have already failed this year.
levels.why: The war has made fuel more expensive, so peace would be welcome news for families.

levels.headline: America says its war with Iran is nearly over, but Iran says no
levels.body:
There has been a war between America and Iran for many months. This week the American president, Donald Trump, said it could end soon. He said he thought there would be no more attacks. But he said he could still attack if he had to.
Iran said no. It said no meeting was planned. Iran says America must do some things first, and it has made a list of seven.
America's top diplomat, Marco Rubio, said talks had not got anywhere. A small country called Qatar is helping the two sides talk, but it said it could not tell if a deal was close.
The war has made oil harder to get, because oil ships must pass through a narrow sea. That has made petrol cost more.
levels.why: If the war ends, oil and petrol could get cheaper for families.

levels.headline: A big argument between two countries, and what was said this week
levels.body:
America and Iran are two countries that have been fighting. It is a bit like a very big, very serious argument that has gone on for months. This week the leader of America, Donald Trump, said the fighting could stop soon. He said he did not expect more attacks.
But Iran said it was not talking to America at all. Iran said America must do some things first before there can be any talks. They have not agreed on much.
It matters to everyone because oil, which makes petrol, travels by ship through a narrow sea near Iran. During the fighting the ships have been in danger, and that has made oil cost more.
Some people hope the argument ends. Others think it could start again.
levels.why: If the fighting stops, it might help fuel get cheaper for families.

levels.headline: Two countries have been fighting, and one says it will stop soon
levels.body:
Imagine two children who have been having a big quarrel in the playground for a very long time. Other children have been caught up in it, and some can't get past.
This week, one of them said the quarrel was almost over. The other said they weren't even talking yet. They still don't agree on how to stop.
The two are the countries America and Iran. A leader called a president, Donald Trump, spoke for America. Because ships near Iran carry oil to the whole world, the quarrel has made things like petrol cost more.
A friend called Qatar is trying to help them talk. Lots of people hope they make friends again soon.
levels.why: If they stop quarrelling, petrol and bills could cost less for families.

headline: Oil edges up from a two-month low as Hormuz shipping attacks offset hopes of an Iran truce

terms.meaning: The main international price benchmark for oil, set in barrels.
A narrow sea route in the Gulf through which a large share of the world's oil ships.
When there is more supply of something than buyers need.

levels.headline: Oil edges up from a two-month low as Hormuz shipping attacks offset hopes of an Iran truce
levels.body:
Oil prices rose on Wednesday 11 November after falling to two-month lows the previous day. Brent futures gained 71 cents, or 0.78%, to $92.20 a barrel, and US West Texas Intermediate rose 49 cents, or 0.57%, to $86.53. On Tuesday Brent briefly dipped below $90 for the first time since August.
Prices have been pulled down by President Donald Trump's remarks that new strikes on Iran are unlikely, while attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz keep supply worries alive. Brent plunged 16% last week, its steepest weekly fall since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. Trading Economics says crude is still about 41% higher than a year ago.
Analysts disagree. Rapidan Energy's Bob McNally puts an 80% probability on fighting resuming, which could send both benchmarks above $100. JPMorgan says the return of Gulf supply has pushed the global market back into surplus after months of disruption.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and the price of almost everything, so they influence inflation and interest rates.

levels.headline: Oil rebounds slightly from a two-month low as Hormuz attacks cloud hopes of an Iran truce
levels.body:
Oil rose a little on Wednesday 11 November after touching two-month lows on Tuesday. Brent crude was up 71 cents, or 0.78%, at $92.20 a barrel, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate gained 49 cents, or 0.57%, to $86.53. On Tuesday Brent briefly slipped under $90, a level last seen in August.
The slide came as Donald Trump played down the chance of fresh strikes on Iran, even though attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz continue to threaten supplies. Brent fell 16% last week, its sharpest weekly drop since the pandemic began, but is still around 41% above a year ago.
Forecasts differ. Rapidan Energy's Bob McNally sees an 80% chance that fighting resumes and prices top $100. JPMorgan argues that returning Gulf supply has put the market back in surplus after months of disruption.
levels.why: Fuel and energy costs shape household bills and the Bank of England's task of controlling inflation.

levels.headline: Oil prices tick up after hitting a two-month low
levels.body:
Oil prices rose slightly on Wednesday 11 November, one day after dropping to their lowest in two months. Brent crude, the world benchmark, gained 71 cents to $92.20 a barrel. The US benchmark rose 49 cents to $86.53. On Tuesday, Brent briefly fell below $90 for the first time since August.
Prices have dropped because President Trump said new strikes on Iran were unlikely. But attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil, are still worrying traders. Last week Brent fell 16%, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the pandemic, though it is still around 41% higher than a year ago.
Experts disagree about what comes next. One, Bob McNally, thinks fighting is likely to restart and send prices above $100. JPMorgan says supplies are returning, leaving the world with more oil than it needs.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can lower petrol and energy prices, but the risk of renewed conflict could push them up again.

levels.headline: Oil prices rise slightly after falling to their lowest level in two months
levels.body:
Oil prices went up a little on Wednesday 11 November, after falling to a two-month low a day earlier. A barrel of Brent crude, the main international price, rose to $92.20. On Tuesday it briefly dropped below $90 for the first time since August.
Oil has been getting cheaper because President Trump said new attacks on Iran are unlikely and hopes of a truce have grown. But ships in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route that much of the world's oil passes through, are still being attacked. That keeps some traders nervous. Last week oil fell 16%, its biggest weekly drop since the pandemic began.
One expert thinks fighting may start again and send prices over $100. Another view, from JPMorgan, is that there is now more oil than buyers need.
levels.why: The price of oil affects what you pay for petrol, energy and many goods in the shops.

levels.headline: Oil prices tick up, but remain near a two-month low
levels.body:
The price of oil rose a little on Wednesday 11 November. But it is still close to its lowest in two months. A barrel of Brent oil, the main world price, cost $92.20. On Tuesday it dipped below $90 for the first time since August.
Why has it fallen? The American president, Donald Trump, said new attacks on Iran are unlikely. People hoped the war might end. But ships are still being attacked in the Strait of Hormuz. This is a narrow stretch of water where lots of the world's oil travels by ship. If the ships cannot pass, oil becomes harder to get, and prices rise.
Experts disagree. One thinks fighting will start again. Another says there is now more oil than the world needs.
levels.why: Oil prices change what we pay for fuel and bills, and how quickly prices rise generally.

levels.headline: Oil gets a little dearer after a big fall earlier this week
levels.body:
The price of oil rose a little on Wednesday 11 November, after it fell to its lowest level in two months. A barrel of Brent oil, the main world price, now costs about $92. It briefly went below $90 on Tuesday.
Oil has become cheaper because the American president, Donald Trump, said new attacks on Iran are unlikely. People hoped the war would end. But ships are still being attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route where a lot of the world's oil is shipped. That keeps some people worried that oil could become hard to get.
Experts disagree. One thinks the fighting will return and push the price above $100. Another says there is now more oil than the world needs.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can bring down petrol and energy costs, but conflict can quickly push them up again.

levels.headline: Oil gets a little dearer after a big fall
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid that is turned into petrol, diesel and heating fuel. Its price went up a little on Wednesday 11 November. But last week it fell a lot, by 16%. That was its biggest fall in a week since 2020.
One price for oil is called Brent. It is now about $92 for a barrel. Earlier this week it briefly went below $90 for the first time since August.
Why the fall? The American president, Donald Trump, said he did not think there would be more attacks on Iran. People hoped the war might end. But ships are still being attacked near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea road for oil tankers. That worries buyers.
Some experts think fighting will come back and prices will rise again. Others say there is plenty of oil now.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can make petrol and energy bills lower, but wars can quickly push them up again.

levels.headline: Oil costs a little more again after getting cheaper
levels.body:
Oil is what we make petrol from. Its price has been going down, but on Wednesday it went up a little. A barrel of oil now costs about $92. It was higher a few weeks ago.
The price fell because people hoped a war between America and Iran might end soon. The American president said more attacks looked unlikely. When people think there will be lots of oil to buy, the price goes down. It is like when a shop has lots of apples, so it sells them cheaper.
But ships carrying oil are still being attacked in a narrow stretch of sea called the Strait of Hormuz. That worries people. If oil is hard to get, it costs more.
levels.why: Oil prices change what petrol costs, and what families pay for fuel and for many other things.

levels.headline: Why oil costs more or less, and what happened this week
levels.body:
Oil is what makes cars and lorries go, and it heats some homes. Oil is dug up in some countries and sent on ships to others. When lots of oil is for sale, the price goes down. When it is hard to get, the price goes up.
This week the price fell, because people hoped a war would end and ships would travel safely again. On Wednesday the price crept up a little. Ships in one narrow sea, called the Strait of Hormuz, are still being attacked, and that makes people nervous.
A barrel of the oil called Brent costs about $92. Some experts think the war will start again and prices will climb. Others think there is plenty of oil.
levels.why: When oil is cheaper, petrol and bills can cost less, which helps families.

levels.headline: Why the price of fuel goes up and down
levels.body:
Think about a sweet shop. If the shop has lots of sweets, it sells them for less. If a lorry full of sweets is stuck on the road, the sweets cost more, because there are fewer to buy.
Oil is a bit like that. Oil is used to make petrol for cars and to heat buildings. This week, oil got cheaper because people hoped a war far away would stop, so oil could travel safely again. On Wednesday, the price went up a little. Some ships were still being attacked in a narrow stretch of sea where lots of oil travels, and that made people worry.
So the price goes up and down as people hope or worry.
levels.why: When oil gets cheaper, grown-ups may spend less on petrol and heating.

headline: Burnham heads to the 20 November UK-EU summit as the debate over free movement and rejoining grows

terms.meaning: The right of citizens to live and work in any country in a group, such as the EU, without a visa.
The EU area where people can cross borders without passport checks.
Automatically following new EU rules as they change.

levels.headline: Burnham heads to the 20 November UK-EU summit as the debate over free movement and rejoining grows
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will attend a UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November. His government says it will focus on growth and illegal immigration. On the table are a trade deal on food and drink, progress on emissions trading and linking energy systems, a youth experience scheme, and deeper cooperation on immigration.
Mr Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about how immigration has changed since Brexit, and has ruled out joining Schengen or the euro. He has said the most ambitious option would be to go "all the way" and rejoin the EU, but that now is not the time to re-run the referendum. He has called a rejoin referendum in a future manifesto "possible" and has ruled out an early election.
Coverage notes Brussels would require free movement, European Court of Justice jurisdiction and dynamic alignment with EU rules. Nigel Farage called the free movement comments a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain". No outcome is confirmed.
levels.why: The summit could set the direction of UK trade, immigration policy and relations with the EU for years.

levels.headline: Burnham prepares for the UK-EU summit as arguments over free movement and rejoining intensify
levels.body:
Andy Burnham will go to Brussels on 20 November for a UK-EU summit that his government says will focus on growth and illegal immigration. Issues include a food and drink trade deal, emissions trading, linking energy systems, a youth experience scheme and closer cooperation on immigration.
The prime minister has asked for an "honest discussion" about immigration since Brexit and ruled out joining Schengen or the euro. He has said the boldest option would be to rejoin the EU, but that the time is not right to rerun the referendum. A rejoin referendum in a future manifesto is "possible", he says, and he has ruled out a snap election.
Brussels would insist on free movement, the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice and dynamic alignment with EU rules. Nigel Farage described the free movement remarks as a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain". No deal has been confirmed.
levels.why: Decisions made here could shape trade, travel and immigration rules for the UK.

levels.headline: Prime Minister to attend a UK-EU summit as the row over free movement and rejoining grows
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will go to Brussels on 20 November for a summit between the UK and the European Union. His government says it will focus on economic growth and illegal immigration. Ideas include a trade deal on food and drink, work on carbon trading, a youth experience scheme and more cooperation on immigration.
Mr Burnham has asked for an "honest discussion" about how immigration has changed since Brexit. He has ruled out joining the euro or the Schengen area. He says the biggest step would be rejoining the EU, but he does not think it is time for another referendum. He says one in a future manifesto is "possible" and he has ruled out an early election.
The EU says rejoining would mean free movement and following EU rules. Nigel Farage called the idea a betrayal.
levels.why: The talks could change how easy it is for people to trade, travel and work between the UK and Europe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister is going to a UK-EU summit, and people disagree about how close to Europe the UK should be
levels.body:
On 20 November, Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet EU leaders in Brussels. His government says the main topics are growth and illegal immigration. They may talk about easier trade in food and drink, cutting pollution, a scheme for young people to live or work abroad, and working together on immigration.
Mr Burnham wants an "honest discussion" about how immigration has changed since Brexit, the UK's departure from the EU. He has said the UK will not join the euro or the Schengen area, where people cross borders freely. He says rejoining the EU is the biggest option, but he does not want another vote yet.
The EU says rejoining would mean free movement of people and following EU rules. Nigel Farage called the idea a betrayal. Nothing has been agreed.
levels.why: The UK's choices about Europe can affect trade, prices and who can live and work here.

levels.headline: The UK Prime Minister will meet EU leaders, and people argue about how close the UK should be to Europe
levels.body:
The UK left the European Union in what people call Brexit. On 20 November, Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet EU leaders in Brussels to talk about the future. His government says the talks will be about growth and illegal immigration. They might also cover easier trade in food and drink, and a scheme for young people to spend time abroad.
Mr Burnham says he wants an honest talk about how immigration has changed since Brexit. He has said the UK will not use the euro. He has also said rejoining the EU is the biggest possible step, but now is not the time for another vote.
The EU says rejoining would mean free movement, which lets people live and work in any member country. Nigel Farage strongly disagrees with the idea.
levels.why: This could change how easily people and goods move between the UK and Europe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister will talk to EU leaders, and people disagree about going back closer to Europe
levels.body:
The UK left the European Union a few years ago. This is called Brexit. On 20 November, the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will go to Brussels to talk with EU leaders. His government says they will talk about growth and stopping illegal boats and other illegal travel. They may also talk about easier trade in food and drink.
Mr Burnham says he wants an honest talk about how the number of people moving to the UK has changed since Brexit. He says the UK will not join the euro, which is the money many EU countries use.
He says the biggest step would be rejoining, but now is not the time for another vote. The EU says rejoining would mean free movement for people. Nigel Farage strongly disagrees.
levels.why: It matters because the UK's links with Europe affect trade, jobs and travel.

levels.headline: The UK Prime Minister will meet EU leaders for important talks
levels.body:
The UK used to be part of a group of European countries called the EU. It left a few years ago. This is called Brexit. On 20 November, the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will meet leaders of the EU in a city called Brussels.
He wants to talk about helping the economy grow and stopping people from coming to the UK illegally. They may also talk about easier trade in food and drink.
Some people want the UK to be closer to the EU again. Others do not. Mr Burnham said the biggest step would be to join again, but he does not think it is time for another vote. Nigel Farage said he strongly disagrees with getting closer.
Nothing has been decided yet.
levels.why: These talks could change how we trade and travel with Europe.

levels.headline: Britain's leader will talk with Europe's leaders
levels.body:
Britain used to be in a team of countries called the European Union, or EU. A few years ago, Britain left the team. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, is going to Brussels on 20 November to talk to the team's leaders.
He wants to talk about making money and jobs grow. He also wants to talk about stopping people who come to Britain in ways that are against the rules.
Some people would like Britain to get closer to the team again. Some do not. The Prime Minister says joining again is the biggest step, but now is not the time to vote on it.
The leaders have not made any decisions yet. They will just talk.
levels.why: What they agree could change how we shop, travel and work with our neighbours.

levels.headline: A leader goes to talk to old friends
levels.body:
Imagine Britain was in a club with lots of other countries in Europe. Then Britain left the club. Some people were happy about that. Others were sad. Now, the leader of Britain, Andy Burnham, is going to visit the club to talk about how to be friends again.
He wants to talk about helping everyone earn more money and about people coming to Britain in ways that break the rules. He does not want to rejoin the club yet, and he says there would need to be another vote first.
Some people want to be closer friends with the club. Some do not. No one has decided anything yet. First they need to talk.
levels.why: Being friends with our neighbours can make shopping, travel and jobs easier.

levels.headline: A leader visits our neighbours to talk
levels.body:
Britain has neighbours in Europe. A while ago, Britain left a big group of them, called the EU. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will visit them on 20 November to talk.
He wants to talk about helping everyone earn money and about people who come to Britain in ways that break the rules. He might also talk about food. Britain and its neighbours may be able to sell food to each other more easily.
Some people want Britain to be closer to its neighbours again. Others want to stay as we are. Mr Burnham says that if Britain ever joined again, there should be another vote first.
No one has decided anything yet. They will start by talking, like friends do.
levels.why: Good talks with neighbours can make things easier for families.

headline: Four EU countries defy Merz as he ties the next EU budget to new Ukraine funding

terms.meaning: The power to block a decision, which in the EU often needs every member country to agree.
Money borrowed together by EU countries, with all of them responsible for repaying it.
The EU's long-term spending plan, agreed by member countries.

levels.headline: Four EU countries defy Merz as he ties the next EU budget to new Ukraine funding
levels.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has told European Council President António Costa, in a letter, that fresh funding for Ukraine is an "essential prerequisite" for approving the EU's next long-term budget. He also wants a lasting arrangement that covers interest already owed on the existing €90 billion loan.
Kyiv faces a shortfall of about €70 billion. The EU has promised to cover two-thirds of it, roughly €45 billion, through an instrument not yet defined, with a new round of joint debt emerging as the frontrunner.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico called the move a "textbook case of blackmail" and threatened a veto. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria also resisted, and the four want to opt out of any future loan to Ukraine. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš noted that money from the budget would not be available until 2028. Costa has sought to reassure Merz, saying both issues will be discussed at a special summit in Brussels at the end of the month.
levels.why: How Europe funds Ukraine and its own budget affects EU unity, spending and the war.

levels.headline: Merz links EU budget to Ukraine aid and meets resistance from four member states
levels.body:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has written to European Council President António Costa saying new Ukraine funding is an "essential prerequisite" for approving the EU's next long-term budget. He also wants a lasting deal covering interest already built up on the existing €90 billion loan.
Ukraine faces a gap of roughly €70 billion. The EU has promised to cover two-thirds, about €45 billion, through an instrument still to be decided, and fresh joint borrowing is the leading option.
Slovakia's Robert Fico called the demand "blackmail" and threatened a veto. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria also pushed back, and the four want to stay out of any future Ukraine loan. Andrej Babiš pointed out that the budget money would not arrive until 2028. António Costa has tried to calm matters, saying both topics will be taken up at a special Brussels summit at the end of the month.
levels.why: The row tests whether EU countries can agree on both their own finances and support for Ukraine.

levels.headline: Germany's chancellor says there will be no EU budget without new money for Ukraine
levels.body:
Germany's chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has told the head of the European Council, António Costa, that the EU cannot agree its next long-term budget unless it first agrees fresh funding for Ukraine. He also wants a lasting plan to deal with interest owed on an existing €90 billion loan.
Ukraine is short of about €70 billion. The EU has said it will cover about two-thirds of that, around €45 billion, but has not decided how. Borrowing together, known as joint debt, looks the most likely method.
Four countries disagree. Slovakia's leader, Robert Fico, called it "blackmail" and said he might use his veto. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria also objected. Costa said the issues will be discussed at a special summit in Brussels later this month.
levels.why: The argument could delay the EU's budget and Ukraine's access to help.

levels.headline: Germany ties the EU budget to help for Ukraine, and four countries push back
levels.body:
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has said the European Union should not approve its next long-term budget until it agrees new money for Ukraine. He wrote to the head of the European Council, António Costa, to say so. He also wants a plan for interest on an older €90 billion loan.
Ukraine needs about €70 billion more. The EU has said it will pay about two-thirds of this, roughly €45 billion, but it has not said how. Borrowing together looks likely.
Four countries are unhappy: Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria. Slovakia's leader, Robert Fico, called the demand "blackmail" and said he may block it with a veto. Costa said the issue will be talked about at a special meeting in Brussels at the end of this month.
levels.why: Decisions about Ukraine and the EU's money affect Europe's security and every member country's spending.

levels.headline: Germany says no deal on Ukraine money means no EU budget, and some countries are angry
levels.body:
Friedrich Merz, the leader of Germany, wants the European Union to agree to give Ukraine more money before it agrees its big spending plan for the coming years. He wrote to the head of the European Council, António Costa, to say this. The EU budget is the plan for how the countries spend money together.
Ukraine is missing about €70 billion. The EU has promised about two-thirds of that, which is roughly €45 billion, but not decided how to find it. One idea is for countries to borrow together.
Four countries do not like Mr Merz's plan. Slovakia's Robert Fico called it "blackmail" and said he might use his veto, which is the power to say no and block a decision. The leaders will talk about it at the end of the month.
levels.why: The EU needs every country to agree, so this argument could slow help for Ukraine.

levels.headline: Germany wants Ukraine money agreed before the EU budget, and four countries disagree
levels.body:
The European Union is a group of countries that share a big spending plan, called the EU budget. Germany's leader, Friedrich Merz, now says the plan should not be agreed until the EU has promised more money to Ukraine, which is fighting a war.
Ukraine is short of about €70 billion. The EU has promised to pay about two-thirds of this. It has not yet worked out how. One idea is to borrow money together.
Four EU countries, Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria, do not like this. Slovakia's leader, Robert Fico, called it "blackmail". He said he might use his veto, which means the power to stop a decision.
The EU's leaders will talk about it at a special meeting in Brussels at the end of the month.
levels.why: EU countries have to agree for anything to happen, so arguments like this can slow things down.

levels.headline: A big argument in Europe about money for Ukraine
levels.body:
The EU is a group of countries that work together. They share a plan for how to spend money, which is called the EU budget. Germany's leader, Friedrich Merz, says that plan should wait until the countries agree to give Ukraine more money. Ukraine is a country that is in a war and needs help to pay its bills.
Ukraine is short of about €70 billion. The EU says it will pay about two-thirds of it, but has not decided how. One idea is for the countries to borrow together.
Four countries disagree. One leader called the plan "blackmail". He said he might use a veto, which means the power to say no and stop it. The leaders will talk about it again at the end of the month.
levels.why: Countries that work together have to agree, and this argument shows how hard that can be.

levels.headline: Countries in Europe argue about how to share money
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe are in a group called the EU. They put money into a pot and agree together how to spend it. This week the leader of Germany, Friedrich Merz, said the group should first agree to help another country, Ukraine, before they agree how to spend the pot.
Ukraine is in a war. It needs about €70 billion, which is a very big amount of money. The EU says it will give about two-thirds of that, but has not worked out where the money will come from.
Four countries said no to Mr Merz's idea. One leader called it unfair and said he might say no to the whole plan. Everyone will talk about it again at the end of the month.
levels.why: When a group has to agree, one disagreement can hold everyone up.

levels.headline: Friends argue about how to share money to help someone
levels.body:
Imagine a class where everyone puts pocket money in a jar to pay for class trips. The class also wants to help a friend from another school who is in trouble and needs money.
One child, called Friedrich, says, "We should not decide about the class trips until we agree to help our friend." Some of the other children do not like this. One says it is unfair, like being told what to do. They each have a say, and if one says no, nothing can happen.
In real life, the class is a group of countries called the EU, and the friend is Ukraine. Ukraine is in a war and needs a lot of money. The leaders will talk again at the end of the month.
levels.why: When people share money, they sometimes disagree about what to do first.

levels.headline: Some countries disagree about helping a friend
levels.body:
There is a group of countries in Europe that share money in a big jar. They want to use some of it to help a country called Ukraine. Ukraine is having a hard time because of a war.
One leader, called Friedrich, said, "Let's agree to help Ukraine first. Then we can agree how to use the rest of the jar." Four other countries did not like being told what to do. One said it was unfair.
It is a bit like when a group of friends cannot agree where to go for lunch. Nobody moves until everyone says yes.
The leaders will meet again at the end of the month to try to agree. Many people hope they will find a way to help.
levels.why: Working together is hard, but it matters when someone needs help.

headline: Race to replace Christine Lagarde at the ECB heats up, with two nominees in the running

terms.meaning: The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the 21 euro countries.
A person put forward for a job.
The EU body of national leaders, which takes the final decision on this appointment.

levels.headline: Race to replace Christine Lagarde at the ECB heats up, with two nominees in the running
levels.body:
Christine Lagarde will step down as President of the European Central Bank on 7 February next year, nearly nine months before her term ends in October 2027. The race to succeed her has two official nominees: Pablo Hernández de Cos, General Manager of the Bank for International Settlements, and Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank.
Spain's economy minister, Carlos Cuerpo, has made the case for Hernández de Cos, who is Spanish. Finance ministers were due to review the names on 9 November. Under the EU process, the European Council takes the decision on the basis of a Council recommendation.
The ECB sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro, so who leads it will help decide how it responds to inflation and economic shocks. Euronews paired the story with news that the EU is joining Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi, but the sources do not link the two.
levels.why: The head of the ECB influences borrowing costs and prices for hundreds of millions of people in the euro area.

levels.headline: Two candidates emerge as the search for Lagarde's successor at the ECB accelerates
levels.body:
Christine Lagarde will leave the presidency of the European Central Bank on 7 February, almost nine months before her term is due to end in October 2027. Two candidates have been formally nominated to replace her: Pablo Hernández de Cos, who runs the Bank for International Settlements, and Klaas Knot, formerly governor of the Dutch central bank.
Spain's economy minister Carlos Cuerpo has backed Hernández de Cos. Finance ministers were scheduled to look at the names on 9 November. The final decision will be taken by the European Council after a Council recommendation.
The ECB sets interest rates across the euro area, so its next president will shape the response to inflation and slowdowns. Euronews covered the race in a daily briefing alongside the Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, though nothing links them.
levels.why: The ECB's leadership affects mortgage rates, savings and prices across the euro area.

levels.headline: Two people are in the running to take over from Christine Lagarde at the European Central Bank
levels.body:
Christine Lagarde is leaving her job as head of the European Central Bank on 7 February next year. That is almost nine months before her term was due to end. Two people have been officially put forward to replace her. One is Pablo Hernández de Cos, who leads the Bank for International Settlements. The other is Klaas Knot, who used to run the Dutch central bank.
Spain's economy minister, Carlos Cuerpo, supports Hernández de Cos. Finance ministers were due to discuss the names on 9 November. The final choice will be made by the European Council, which brings together EU leaders.
The ECB sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro, so its leader matters for prices and loans.
levels.why: The person chosen will help set interest rates for the euro area, which affects trade with the UK too.

levels.headline: The search for a new head of the European Central Bank is under way
levels.body:
Christine Lagarde will stop being the president of the European Central Bank on 7 February next year, nearly nine months early. Two names are officially in the race to replace her. They are Pablo Hernández de Cos, who works at the Bank for International Settlements, and Klaas Knot, a former head of the Dutch central bank.
Spain's economy minister, Carlos Cuerpo, has said he supports Hernández de Cos. Ministers who look after finance in the EU countries were due to look at the names on 9 November. EU leaders, meeting as the European Council, will make the final decision.
The ECB decides interest rates for the countries that use the euro. That makes the choice important for prices and loans in Europe.
levels.why: A new boss can change the way interest rates are set for millions of people.

levels.headline: Who will lead the European Central Bank next? Two people are in the race
levels.body:
The European Central Bank, or ECB, is the bank in charge of money for the countries that use the euro. Its boss, Christine Lagarde, will leave on 7 February next year. That is nearly nine months before her job was due to end.
Two people have been put forward to take over. One is Pablo Hernández de Cos, who comes from Spain and now works at an international bank for banks. The other is Klaas Knot, who used to run the central bank of the Netherlands.
Spain's economy minister supports Hernández de Cos. Ministers from across the EU were due to talk about the two names on 9 November. Then EU leaders will decide.
The ECB sets interest rates, which affect the cost of borrowing.
levels.why: The ECB's boss helps decide how expensive loans are across Europe.

levels.headline: Two people want to run Europe's central bank after Christine Lagarde leaves
levels.body:
Many European countries use the same money, the euro. A bank called the European Central Bank, or ECB, looks after it. Its boss, Christine Lagarde, will leave her job on 7 February next year. That is earlier than planned.
Two people have been put forward to take over. Pablo Hernández de Cos is from Spain. Klaas Knot used to be in charge of the central bank in the Netherlands. A minister from Spain says Mr Hernández de Cos would be a good choice.
Ministers from EU countries have been talking about the two names. In the end, the leaders of the EU countries will choose.
The ECB sets interest rates, which are the cost of borrowing money. That is why people care who gets the job.
levels.why: The boss of the ECB can change how much it costs people in Europe to borrow money.

levels.headline: Europe is choosing a new boss for the bank that looks after the euro
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe use the same money. It is called the euro. A special bank looks after it. It is called the European Central Bank. The boss of this bank is a woman called Christine Lagarde, and she will leave her job in February.
Now the countries need to pick a new boss. Two people have been put forward. One is called Pablo Hernández de Cos, from Spain. The other is called Klaas Knot, from the Netherlands. A minister from Spain said Mr Hernández de Cos would do a good job.
The leaders of the countries will choose in the end. The boss helps decide how expensive it is to borrow money, so it is an important job.
levels.why: The new boss will help decide how much people pay when they borrow money.

levels.headline: Choosing a new boss for a very important bank
levels.body:
Some countries in Europe share the same money, called the euro. A big bank looks after it. This bank has a boss called Christine Lagarde. She is going to leave in February.
So the countries need to find a new boss. Two people have been picked as possible choices. They are called Pablo and Klaas. Pablo comes from Spain and Klaas comes from the Netherlands. A minister from Spain said Pablo would be good.
The leaders of the countries will vote, a bit like choosing a new class captain. The bank boss helps decide how much extra people must pay when they borrow money, so lots of people care about who is picked.
levels.why: It is a big job that can change how much money costs to borrow.

levels.headline: Picking a new captain for a team
levels.body:
Imagine a team of many players from different countries. They all use the same kind of coins. The team has a captain called Christine, and the captain looks after the coins and helps decide how much extra to pay when you borrow from the team.
Christine is going to stop being captain in February. Now the team needs a new one. Two players have been picked as choices. One is called Pablo and comes from Spain. The other is called Klaas and comes from the Netherlands.
The team leaders will decide, like voting for a class captain. Everyone wants to pick someone good, because the captain's job matters to the whole team.
levels.why: A captain who makes good choices helps the whole team, and a bank boss helps lots of people.

levels.headline: A team needs a new leader
levels.body:
Think of a big team that looks after the money for lots of countries. The team's leader is called Christine. She has been doing the job for a while, and she has decided to leave in February.
Now the team needs someone new. Two people have been put forward. One is Pablo, who is from Spain. The other is Klaas, who is from the Netherlands.
The grown-ups in charge will talk about them and then choose, like when your school picks a new head girl or head boy.
The leader of this team makes choices about money. Those choices can make things a little cheaper or a little dearer for families.
levels.why: A good leader helps keep things fair and steady for lots of families.

headline: Supreme Court hears Palestine Action appeal against its ban, with a ruling still awaited

terms.meaning: A government ban that makes it a crime to belong to or support a group.
The highest court in the UK for most cases.
A court case that checks whether a public body acted lawfully.

levels.headline: Supreme Court hears Palestine Action appeal against its ban, with a ruling still awaited
levels.body:
The UK Supreme Court heard Huda Ammori's appeal against the ban on Palestine Action over two days, 4 and 5 November, in an expedited hearing. No judgment has been published yet. Police arrested 25 people outside the court on 4 November on suspicion of supporting a proscribed organisation.
Ms Ammori was granted permission to challenge the ban on a narrow procedural ground: that the Home Office failed to follow its own criteria. Her team will also argue that only three of the 385 actions carried out by the group over five years were assessed as meeting the legal definition of terrorism.
The High Court ruled in February that the ban was "disproportionate", but the Court of Appeal reversed that in June, finding the decision was not unlawful. If she loses, Ms Ammori has said she will go to the European Court of Human Rights. Charges linked to the ban could be affected if the appeal succeeds.
levels.why: The ruling will decide whether supporting the group remains a crime and how far ministers can use anti-terror powers.

levels.body:

levels.headline: The Supreme Court has listened to arguments about the ban on Palestine Action
levels.body:
The Supreme Court is the highest court in the UK. On 4 and 5 November it listened to an appeal about the government's ban on a group called Palestine Action. The government banned the group using terrorism laws, so it became a crime to support it. Huda Ammori is trying to have the ban removed. The court has not given its answer yet. Police arrested 25 people outside the court on 4 November for supporting a banned group.
Ms Ammori can only argue that the Home Office did not follow its own rules. Her lawyers say just three of the group's 385 actions over five years counted as terrorism.
Earlier courts disagreed with each other. If she loses, she says she will go to a European court.
